h1: Olive Oil Shelf Life: How Long a Bottle Really Lasts
excerpt: Olive oil shelf life is decided by air, light and heat rather than by the date printed on the bottle, and a Malaysian kitchen runs harder on a bottle than a Mediterranean pantry does.
keyTakeaway: Olive oil shelf life runs up to about eighteen months from harvest while the bottle is sealed, and about two months of real character once the cap comes off. Air, light and heat set that pace, not the printed date. Read the harvest date, store the bottle dark and away from the stove, and buy the size your kitchen finishes.

intro: Olive oil does not spoil the way milk spoils. It fades. The fruit goes first, then the pepper at the back of the throat, and one afternoon the bottle tastes of nothing much.
Here is what a bottle has in it, unopened and opened, what ends it, and why a Selangor kitchen is harder on oil than a Mediterranean pantry.

sections.heading: How long a bottle lasts, unopened and opened

blocks.text: An unopened bottle of extra virgin olive oil typically holds its character for up to about eighteen months from the harvest that produced it, kept cool and dark. Once opened, count in weeks rather than seasons: about two months of real character is a fair expectation, because air is now inside for good.

A harvest date tells you when the olives were milled. A best-before date tells you when the bottler stopped guaranteeing the oil, counted from the bottling run, which can happen months after the fruit was pressed. Where both appear, read the harvest date first and treat the other as an outer limit.

items: **Harvest or crush date.** The real age of the oil in the bottle.
**Best before.** Counted from bottling, not from the mill.
**Lot code.** Useful to a recall, not to you.
**No date at all.** Common on blends, and a reason to ask.

blocks.text: For the rest of what belongs on a label you are about to pay for, read [how to choose authentic extra virgin olive oil in Malaysia](/blog/how-to-choose-authentic-extra-virgin-olive-oil-in-malaysia).

sections.heading: Air, light and heat are what end a bottle

blocks.text: Three things end a bottle. Air enters every time the cap comes off and stays in the space above the oil. Light drives the same reaction faster, which is the reason dark glass exists. Heat multiplies both. Sealed, cold and dark, an oil barely moves at all.

sections.heading: Why a Malaysian kitchen is the harder environment

blocks.text: A Malaysian kitchen runs warm and humid every month of the year, with no cold season to give a bottle a rest. Indoor temperatures sit near 28°C before anyone lights the hob, and an open layout puts the oil in daylight for hours. A Mediterranean pantry spends part of the year cold.

Two habits cover most of the risk. Keep the bottle in a closed cupboard on the far side of the kitchen from the hob, never on the shelf above it, and screw the cap back down the moment the pouring is done.

sections.heading: How to tell an oil has gone

blocks.text: Pour a little into a spoon and smell it before you taste it. A finished oil smells of wax crayon, putty, stale nuts or damp cardboard, and tastes greasy and flat with no peppery catch at the back of the throat. Cloudiness alone is not a fault; a cold bottle clouds and clears again.

items: **Smell.** Crayon or putty where fruit used to be.
**Taste.** Flat and greasy, the peppery finish gone.
**Colour.** Duller and browner than the day it was opened.
**Sediment.** Normal in unfiltered oil; a musty smell with it is not.

sections.heading: Bottle size is a shelf-life decision

blocks.text: Buy the size your kitchen will finish, not the size with the better price per litre. A household that reaches for olive oil twice a week takes months over 500 ml, and the last third tastes nothing like the first pour. The same oil in 250 ml is used while it still has everything.
Both sizes sit on the [products page](/products), and what separates them by the litre is set out in [olive oil price in Malaysia](/blog/olive-oil-price-in-malaysia-what-you-are-paying-for).

Sealed and cool, up to about eighteen months from harvest. Opened, about two months of real character. Air, light and heat decide which end you get. Read the harvest date and buy the size you will finish.

faqs.q: How long does olive oil last unopened?
faqs.a: Kept cool and dark, an unopened bottle typically holds its character for up to about eighteen months from the harvest that produced it. The seal keeps air out, so a sealed bottle ages far more slowly than an opened one standing on a counter.

faqs.q: How long does olive oil last after opening?
faqs.a: About two months is a fair figure for a bottle in regular use in Malaysia. Air enters the space above the oil every time the cap comes off, so a half-empty bottle left for weeks ages faster than one poured from daily.

faqs.q: Does olive oil go bad, or just go stale?
faqs.a: It goes stale rather than spoiling. Oxidation flattens the fruit and the pepper and leaves a waxy, cardboard smell. The oil is still oil, but the character you paid for has gone. That is why a harvest date beats an expiry date.

faqs.q: Should olive oil be kept in the fridge?
faqs.a: It is not necessary, and cold oil is awkward to pour. It clouds and thickens, then clears again at room temperature with nothing lost. A closed cupboard away from the stove does the same job for a bottle finished within a few months.

faqs.q: Can I use olive oil after the best-before date?
faqs.a: A best-before date is a limit set by the bottler, not a hard stop. Smell and taste the oil first. If it is flat or smells of crayon, cook with it in a spiced dish and open a fresh bottle for salads.

faqs.q: Which bottle size keeps better once opened?
faqs.a: Neither keeps better; the smaller one gets finished sooner, which comes to the same thing. A 250 ml bottle suits a kitchen that pours olive oil now and then, and a 500 ml bottle suits one that cooks with it most days.
